This isn’t a wharf closure, it’s a decision about who the valley is for.

On Tuesday the council voted to shut the old cargo wharf at Stannard Lock to commercial boats from next spring. Nobody asked the growers first. Our co-op moves about nine hundred tonnes of fruit a season down that canal — every crate of it lands at that wharf.

If the barges stop, the fruit goes by road. That means something like sixty extra lorry trips through lanes that were never built for them. The lanes are narrow, the verges are soft after rain, and two lorries cannot pass each other near the chapel without one of them backing up. It also means more bruised apples, because a crate on a lorry shakes all the way to the press and a crate on the water barely moves.

The ramp is not a luxury, it’s the cheapest answer we have. There is a second wharf four hundred metres upstream. With a small loading ramp it could take our barges, and the materials would cost about eighteen thousand. The labour would be ours, two weeks of it, the way we have built most things here. We have done it before. The tug's charging point on the lock keeper's cottage went up in a fortnight, and the panels have run every season since without a fault. A ramp is a smaller job than that, and the growers already have the tools and the timber.

I think the council saw a quiet wharf and assumed it was an empty one. It is quiet because the tug is electric and the crew of two do not shout. The wharf is busy every October and most of November. On a good morning four barges wait at the lock, and the press at the bottom of the valley runs until the last crate is in. The growers count on that rhythm, and so do the pickers who come back to the orchards every year.

We have nineteen orchards in the co-op, each with one share and one vote — and every one of them will be at the meeting on the first Thursday of next month. I would like the council to come too. We will bring the waste figures from last season, weighed crate by crate at the press. We will show them the bruising figures, the lorry counts and the plan for the ramp, and we will ask them to give us one season to build it.

If you live on the lanes between Hollin Vale and the main road, you have a stake in this as well. Sixty lorries a season would pass your gate, most of them in the weeks when the lanes are busiest with school traffic and harvest tractors. Come to the meeting, or write to your councillor before then. The barges have carried this valley's fruit for eleven years, and I would like them to carry it for eleven more.
